name: Bryce Canyon National Park
blurb: Pine forest, prairie dogs and mountain lions above the hoodoos.

tip.title: Remove the prairie dogs
tip.text: Prairie dogs mix the soil and feed hawks and snakes. Set Utah prairie dog to -100% and watch the meadow grass, then the hawk and rattlesnake.

sources.title: National Park Service: Bryce Canyon animals

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Strong high-elevation sunlight powers the short growing season of the plateau forests and meadows.

nodes.name: Snowmelt and summer rain
nodes.desc: The park receives roughly 15 to 18 inches of precipitation a year, more than nearby Zion, and it feeds the plateau's trees and meadows.

nodes.name: Soil and soil crust
nodes.desc: Crusts of lichens, algae, fungi and cyanobacteria slow erosion, add nitrogen and help soil hold moisture.

nodes.name: Fungi and bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead wood, leaves, droppings and carcasses, returning nutrients to the soil.

nodes.name: Ponderosa pine
nodes.desc: The main tree of the park's middle elevations. Clark's nutcrackers and jays eat its seeds, and GloBI records nutcrackers doing so.

nodes.name: Limber pine
nodes.desc: A high-elevation white pine with large seeds that Clark's nutcracker eats and caches.

nodes.name: Quaking aspen
nodes.desc: A leafy tree of the park's highest, coolest areas, listed on Wikipedia with Douglas fir and blue spruce there.

nodes.name: Native grasses
nodes.desc: Grasses of the meadows are a main food of Utah prairie dogs, which favour a few native grass species.

nodes.name: Showy green gentian
nodes.desc: A tall flowering plant of mountain meadows. GloBI records Hunt's bumble bee feeding on it.

nodes.name: Mule deer
nodes.desc: A common large grazer and browser of the park, recorded in numbers by GBIF and eaten by mountain lions.

nodes.name: Pronghorn
nodes.desc: Crosses the forested plateau and open ground in search of food and water, according to the park service.

nodes.name: Utah prairie dog
nodes.desc: A threatened burrowing rodent reintroduced to the park. Wikipedia calls it a keystone species because its burrowing mixes soil and its burrows shelter other animals.

nodes.name: Uinta chipmunk
nodes.desc: The most recorded mammal near the park. A small forest rodent that feeds mainly on seeds and is prey for hawks.

nodes.name: Deer mouse
nodes.desc: A small seed- and insect-eating rodent and a frequent prey of hawks and snakes in GloBI records.

nodes.name: Clark's nutcracker
nodes.desc: Feeds mainly on pine seeds, caches more than it needs, and also eats insects and carrion. It helps spread limber and whitebark pines.

nodes.name: Hunt's bumble bee
nodes.desc: A bumble bee that gathers nectar and pollen from mountain wildflowers, and is a pollinator.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.desc: The most recorded bird near the park. An opportunist that scavenges carrion and takes small animals.

nodes.name: Turkey vulture
nodes.desc: A scavenging bird; GloBI records it feeding on dead mule deer and rodents.

nodes.name: Red-tailed hawk
nodes.desc: A widespread raptor that hunts rodents, birds and snakes; the GloBI records show many prey species from this area.

nodes.name: Great Basin rattlesnake
nodes.desc: A venomous snake listed among the park's reptiles that hunts small rodents and lizards.

nodes.name: Mountain lion
nodes.desc: The main large predator the park lists. Deer are its chief prey in western mountain country.
